language_wrapper: Let A_1, A_2, ..., A_[n] be the vertices of a regular [n]-gon. How many distinct squares in the plane of the polygon have at least two vertices in the set {A_1, A_2, ..., A_[n]}?
hardness_rationale: The family parameterizes the number of vertices n, requiring a general combinatorial-geometric analysis rather than a single numeric case. The key difficulty is recognizing that each unordered pair of vertices generates exactly three squares (two with the pair as a side and one as a diagonal), and that distinct squares are overcounted precisely through the number of vertex pairs they contain. Crucially, one must prove that a square cannot pass through exactly three polygon vertices; the only multi-vertex overlaps arise from fully inscribed squares, present iff 4 divides n. This global incidence-counting argument and the nontrivial exclusion of the 3-vertex case make the generalized problem substantially deeper than the seed.
notes:
Proof of correctness. Place the regular n-gon on the unit circle. For any unordered pair of distinct vertices P,Q:
- There are exactly two squares having PQ as a side (one on each side of the line PQ).
- There is exactly one square having PQ as a diagonal (the other two vertices are the midpoint of PQ plus/minus a vector perpendicular to PQ of length |PQ|/2). Thus, each pair contributes exactly 3 pair-square incidences, and the total number of incidences is 3*C(n,2).
For a distinct square S that meets s vertices of the set, the number of unordered vertex-pairs contained in S is C(s,2), so S contributes C(s,2) incidences to the global count. Summing over all distinct squares yields 3*C(n,2) = sum_S C(s_S,2).
We claim s_S cannot be 3. Suppose three vertices X,Y,Z of the circle form a right angle at Y. By the inscribed angle theorem, angle XYZ is half the measure of arc XZ not containing Y, so it equals 90 degrees only if X and Z are diametrically opposite. In that case, unless Y is also n/4 steps from both X and Z (which happens exactly when 4|n), the triangle is right but not isosceles. If Y is n/4 from both, the fourth vertex (the other corner of the inscribed square) is also a polygon vertex, so s_S = 4. Hence s_S = 3 is impossible.
Therefore, all overlaps come only from inscribed squares (s_S = 4). An inscribed square exists iff 4|n, and the number of distinct inscribed squares is n/4: starting at any vertex i, the square is {i, i+n/4, i+n/2, i+3n/4}, and each is counted 4 times over starting indices, so distinct squares are n/4.
Let S4 = n/4 if 4|n and 0 otherwise, and let S2 count squares meeting exactly two vertices. From 3*C(n,2) = S2 + 6*S4 and N = S2 + S4, we get N = 3*C(n,2) - 5*S4. This is the claimed formula.
Family explanation: The instance parameter n generalizes the seed dodecagon to any regular n-gon, preserving the core idea (counting squares that pass through at least two designated vertices) but requiring a universal argument that handles overcounting, the diagonal-versus-side distinction, and the impossibility of the 3-vertex case. The final closed form N(n) = 3*C(n,2) - 5*(n/4 if 4|n else 0) captures all instances succinctly.
source_question: Let $A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots, A_{12}$ be the vertices of a regular dodecagon. How many distinct squares in the plane of the dodecagon have at least two vertices in the set $\{A_1,A_2,A_3,\ldots,A_{12}\}$ ?
